messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan was twenty-six, working as a painter for a residential renovation company in Chicago, when he was mugged at gunpoint outside a corner store in his own neighborhood. It was late evening, just after a shift, and he had stopped to buy water. The man came from behind the dumpster, pressed a pistol into his ribs, and demanded his wallet and phone. Rajan handed them over without a word, hands shaking, and the man disappeared into an alley. The whole thing lasted maybe forty seconds. But in the months that followed, Rajan found himself waking from nightmares with a cold dread washing over him, the dream residue leaving him disoriented and afraid, his heart pounding before he even remembered why. Those mornings, he would lie still, trying to reconstruct what had happened, but the memory felt like a torn photograph—he could see the gun, the man's jacket, the dumpster, but the sequence was scrambled, and trying to deliberately recall it only made the gaps feel larger. After the memory surfaced with that raw, disjointed quality, the rest of the day became a minefield—the smell of gasoline at a gas station, the jingle of keys in a pocket, the way a stranger's shadow fell across the pavement—all of it now felt like a signal, as if the memory had seeded the world with warnings. He felt a sickening guilt when he thought about it, a conviction that he should have fought back, should have run, should have done something, and the guilt itself made the memory harder to hold onto, sliding away like water through fingers.

The guilt fed a growing belief that he could not trust anyone—not the strangers on the street, not the neighbors he had known for years, not even his own judgment. He began to feel isolated, set apart from his wife Priya and his coworkers, as if he were living behind a pane of glass. He was certain that people were only pretending to be decent, that underneath they were all capable of violence. This certainty meant that he no longer needed a genuine threat to set off his alarm—a car backfiring, a door slamming in the next apartment, even the sudden ring of a phone could feel like the opening move of another attack, each sound a trigger he couldn't ignore. This belief made him scan for danger constantly, his body perpetually tense, ready to react. Walking to the hardware store for supplies became a tactical operation: he checked every doorway, every parked van, every person who glanced his way. When a customer at a job site made a sudden movement to adjust a ladder, Rajan snapped, shouting at the man before he could stop himself, and the angry flush of adrenaline only reinforced his sense that danger was everywhere, that he was right to be on guard. Already running on that background hum of threat, he found that ordinary cues he would once have ignored—a car slowing as it passed him, a neighbor's hand moving too quickly toward a pocket—now landed as urgent messages, each one demanding his full attention. The scanning itself—the hypervigilance—became a trigger: the sight of a dumpster, the shape of a man's silhouette, the feel of a wallet in his back pocket, all of it could send him back into the fragmented, guilt-ridden loop of the memory.

His avoidance grew quietly. He stopped walking past the corner store, taking a longer route that added twenty minutes to his commute. He stopped going out after dark altogether, telling Priya he was tired. He stopped answering calls from his brother, because talking about his day meant accounting for where he had been, and that meant explaining why he had not been where he used to go. The isolation deepened his belief that he could not rely on others, and that belief made him more watchful, more tense, more likely to interpret a harmless gesture as a threat. And the more he watched, the more he found evidence of danger—a man standing too close on the train platform, a car idling too long on his street—and each new perceived threat triggered another fragment of the memory, another wave of guilt, another reason to pull further away.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment at work. He was painting a bedroom in a client's home, and the client's teenage son came up behind him to ask a question. Rajan spun around, paintbrush raised like a weapon, and the boy stumbled backward, terrified. The client asked him to leave. Priya, who had been watching him withdraw for months, said quietly that night that she could not watch him disappear anymore. Rajan sat in the intake office three days later, unable to say what he hoped for, but certain of one thing: he was afraid that if he let his guard down, even for a second, he would be robbed again, or worse, and this time he would deserve it.
